By defining a quantifiable model discrepancy that captures the behavioral gap between the teacher and student, we derive a mathematically optimizable upper bound. During training, the student and teacher architectures act together as a discriminator to minimize this discrepancy. Concurrently, a generator adversarially synthesizes synthetic hard samples intended to maximize the gap. Comprehensive empirical validations confirm that this data-free approach matches the performance achieved by traditional data-driven baselines. Beyond standard classification tasks, the proposed method easily adapts to the considerably more complex domain of semantic segmentation, where it establishes new state-of-the-art results. Pretrained models and associated code can be found at https://github.com/VainF/Data-Free-Adversarial-Distillation.

author: Martin
title: Knowledge Distillation Using BERT for Sequence-to-Sequence ASR
abstract: Because decoding strictly proceeds left-to-right, conventional attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) architectures for automatic speech recognition (ASR) inherently ignore right context. To incorporate bidirectional information, we utilize an external language model, specifically BERT, and apply knowledge distillation to improve the seq2seq ASR framework. The proposed method trains the ASR network using soft labels output by BERT. We additionally supply BERT with textual histories extending past the current utterance. Experiments conducted on the CSJ (Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese) database demonstrate that our technique achieves substantial performance improvements over a standard seq2seq baseline. Comparisons reveal that knowledge distillation derived from BERT surpasses results obtained using a strictly left-context transformer LM. Incorporating text spanning beyond the current utterance was similarly proven to be highly effective. Ultimately, our approach delivers superior accuracy compared to standard integration schemes like shallow fusion or n-best rescoring, all without adding any extra inference cost.

author: Gray
title: An Ensemble of Projectors for Enhanced Feature Distillation
abstract: While the selection of distilled layers and the formulation of loss functions have dominated prior research in feature distillation, the specific role of the feature projector connecting the student and teacher has received minimal attention. We find that incorporating a projector enhances the student, even in scenarios where the teacher and student share identical feature dimensions. When this module is omitted, optimizing the student backbone acts as a multi-task learning problem, demanding that it simultaneously match teacher features for distillation and extract discriminative features for classification. We provide empirical evidence supporting the hypothesis that lacking a projector causes the student model to overfit the feature distributions of the teacher, regardless of disparities in weight initialization or network architecture. This phenomenon subsequently degrades the deep features of the student network, which are critical for the classification task. Conversely, integrating a projector successfully disentangles these dual objectives. It enables the student to prioritize its primary feature extraction task, while relying on the projector to channel the teacher features for guidance. Building upon these mechanistic insights, we introduce a novel feature distillation technique utilizing an ensemble of projectors to further elevate the quality of the learned representations. Comprehensive experiments across multiple datasets, evaluating a diverse array of teacher-student pairs, confirm that the proposed method consistently achieves superior performance.

author: Mayo
title: Knowledge Distillation and Soft Labels: An Examination of the Bias-Variance Tradeoff
abstract: To guide a student network's training, knowledge distillation utilizes the predictions of a highly optimized teacher network, or an ensemble of teachers, as soft labels. While recent research demonstrates that such soft labels provide valuable regularization for the student, it remains unclear exactly how this practice affects bias and variance, even though statistical regularization fundamentally operates by shrinking variance. This work explores the distillation process through the lens of the bias-variance tradeoff. We reveal that this tradeoff fluctuates on a per-sample basis throughout the training phase. Furthermore, when holding the distillation temperature constant, overall efficacy exhibits a negative correlation with the frequency of certain inputs we classify as regularization samples. We define these specific instances as those that simultaneously reduce variance and inflate bias. Despite this negative association, empirical tests demonstrate that simply discarding these regularization samples severely harms the final distillation performance. Driven by these findings, we introduce a novel adaptive weighting mechanism for soft labels, enabling the student network to dynamically manage the bias-variance tradeoff at the individual sample level. Evaluations across standard benchmark datasets confirm the proposed method's efficacy. Source code can be accessed at https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation.

author: Bowman
title: Compressing Universal Paralinguistic Speech Representations via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: While self-supervision has significantly enhanced speech representations, implementing state-of-the-art embedding models directly on-device remains difficult because they demand massive resources and frequently lack public availability. To overcome these deployment barriers, we publicly release a suite of compact paralinguistic speech models that provide near state-of-the-art performance. Trained exclusively with public data, our approach leverages knowledge distillation across multiple investigated architectures. We comprehensively assess the resulting models using the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. Our largest distilled model occupies under 15% of the original footprint (314MB rather than 2.2GB) and requires just 6.5% of the training data, yet it preserves over 96% of the initial accuracy across 6 out of 7 tasks. Strikingly, our smallest model necessitates merely 1% of the baseline capacity (22MB) while securing greater than 90% accuracy for 6 out of 7 tasks. Overall, the distilled models surpass the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 baseline in 6 out of 7 tasks. Furthermore, despite comprising a mere 7% of the baseline size, our smallest model exceeds the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks.

author: Hawkins
title: Accelerating Knowledge Distillation for Visual Recognition Tasks
abstract: Forward passes through massive teacher networks dominate the computational expense of standard knowledge distillation (KD), rendering the overall training process highly inefficient. This bottleneck persists despite KD being highly effective for supervised classification as well as self-supervised representation learning. To avoid querying teachers multiple times, a recent method named ReLabel pre-computes a full-image label map and extracts region-level labels via RoI align during training. However, this strategy suffers from a drop in accuracy because standard multi-crop training of KD teachers creates inconsistencies between the extracted region-level labels and the global label-map. To address this flaw, we introduce an accelerated distillation framework that directly produces soft labels using a multi-crop KD strategy, exactly mirroring the distillation training phase. By eliminating post-processing steps such as softmax operations and RoI align, our proposed approach operates at higher speeds than ReLabel. Furthermore, integrating multi-crop sampling from a single image during data loading makes our technique strictly more computationally efficient than conventional image classification pipelines. We validate this framework on ImageNet-1K, where a ResNet-50 model reaches 79.8% accuracy. This represents an improvement of ~1.0% over ReLabel, alongside an increase in speed. Additionally, we establish the superior efficiency of our technique in self-supervised learning scenarios. Models, source code, and project details are hosted at http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html and https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

author: Cohen
title: Attention-Guided Combinatorial Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Coupling a compact student network with a highly accurate teacher network during training facilitates effective model compression while maintaining strong performance, a methodology generally known as knowledge distillation. In typical setups, the student exclusively mimics the final predictions of the teacher, completely ignoring the potential supervision available within internal components. Addressing this missed opportunity, our work investigates representation transfer across intermediate layers. Because differing network depths prevent direct one-to-one alignment, conventional distillation approaches simply discard certain teacher layers and extract knowledge from a limited subset. Since this omission degrades final model quality, we introduce an attention-driven combinatorial technique as an alternative. Our proposed method evaluates the significance of each layer to fuse relevant teacher-side information, subsequently performing distillation between these aggregated teacher representations and the corresponding student layers. To evaluate this combinatorial strategy, we compressed a standard BERT architecture of 12 layers (Devlin et al. 2019) into smaller student equivalents containing 2, 4, and 6 layers. Performance measurements on the GLUE evaluation suite (Wang et al. 2018) reveal that our attention-based method yields superior results when compared against existing layer distillation techniques.

author: Cameron
title: Evaluating the Role of Pre-training in Compact Student Architectures
abstract: Self-supervised pre-training on massive corpora has driven tremendous progress in natural language representations, yet the resulting architectures are computationally prohibitive for many down-stream tasks. Consequently, researchers have introduced numerous model compression strategies for these large systems. Curiously, a straightforward baseline is largely ignored by recent studies: applying pre-training followed by fine-tuning to compact models. We demonstrate that establishing this basic approach yields results that rival the more complex techniques seen in contemporary literature, emphasizing that smaller architectures still heavily benefit from pre-training. Furthermore, we explore the use of standard knowledge distillation to transfer the task knowledge learned by massive fine-tuned models into our compact initialized architectures. This straightforward, widely applicable, and effective procedure yields additional performance gains. We also conduct comprehensive experiments to analyze how distillation and pre-training interact, focusing specifically on two rarely examined factors: overall model size and the characteristics of the unlabeled task data. Unexpectedly, combining these two training stages yields a compound effect, which holds true even when both are executed sequentially utilizing the exact same text data. To facilitate ongoing investigation by the community, we are publicly releasing a suite of 24 miniature BERT models that underwent prior pre-training.

author: Parsons
title: Enhancing Dense Retrieval Distillation via Curriculum Learning
abstract: Transferring ranking knowledge from a baseline re-ranking model is a well-established strategy for producing highly capable dense retrieval models. To improve this process, we introduce a generalized optimization strategy based on curriculum learning. By carefully regulating the complexity of the training data generated by the teacher (the re-ranking model), our proposed framework systematically updates the student (the dense retrieval model). Specifically, the knowledge distillation data fed to the student grows increasingly challenging at each iteration. We accomplish this by first supplying the student with broad, coarse-grained preference pairs extracted from the teacher's ranking. As training advances, these pairwise document ordering requirements are gradually shifted toward much finer-grained distinctions. We validate this approach by employing a straightforward implementation to upgrade two distinct dense retrieval architectures that represent the state-of-the-art. Evaluations conducted across three public datasets for passage retrieval confirm that the proposed curriculum learning framework successfully improves retrieval effectiveness.

author: Perez
title: Transferring Single-Task Knowledge into Multi-Task Architectures for Natural Language Understanding
abstract: Exceeding or matching single-task neural networks using multi-task models often proves difficult. To overcome this, we utilize knowledge distillation, wherein dedicated single-task models instruct a multi-task student. We further improve optimization via a novel scheduling routine that slowly shifts the focus away from knowledge distillation toward standard supervised learning. This gradual change empowers the multi-task model to eventually outperform its single-task teachers. We validate the framework by conducting multi-task fine-tuning on BERT across the GLUE benchmark. Contrasted with standard multi-task training or typical single-task approaches, our strategy delivers consistent performance gains.

author: Stewart
title: Achieving Differential Privacy in Model Compression Through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Executing deep neural networks (DNNs) locally is increasingly necessary for modern smartphone applications. Unfortunately, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy requires highly complex architectures that demand far more computational power than mobile platforms can provide. Furthermore, engineering such advanced models depends on aggregating vast quantities of potentially sensitive user information. Consequently, distributing these models to consumer hardware introduces severe security vulnerabilities regarding personal data. To resolve these dual challenges of hardware limitations and data vulnerability, we present a novel private model compression pipeline. By adopting a knowledge distillation approach, our proposed framework simultaneously leverages self learning, hint learning, and distillation learning to optimize a highly efficient, compact neural network. To guarantee differential privacy, we apply targeted perturbations and adaptive bounding to the information extracted from the massive source model. Additionally, we introduce a refined technique for query sample selection that restricts overall privacy loss by minimizing total queries. Extensive experimental validation, including real-world deployment on an Android smartphone, verifies that the proposed method secures sensitive data while successfully shrinking cumbersome models. Specifically, ensuring strict $(9.83, 10^{-6})$-differential privacy during SVHN dataset evaluations, our optimized compact network achieves a 19$\times$ acceleration and a 20$\times$ size reduction, alongside a minimal classification accuracy drop of just 0.97%.

author: Adams
title: An Empirical Investigation into the Alleged Incompatibility of Knowledge Distillation and Label Smoothing
abstract: Recent claims suggest that combining knowledge distillation with label smoothing causes conflicts, prompting this empirical investigation to clarify the issue. The primary justification for this hypothesized incompatibility asserts that relative information distinguishing the teacher logits is eliminated by label smoothing. To explore this dynamic, we present a new theoretical link demonstrating how applying label smoothing alters the underlying distributions of classes that are semantically similar versus dissimilar ones. Furthermore, we introduce a quantitative metric designed to assess exactly how much information disappears from a given sample's representation. Through exhaustive evaluations across Neural Machine Translation, Binary Networks, and Image Classification, coupled with extensive visualizations and in-depth analyses, we demonstrate that the aforementioned perspective of incompatibility remains flawed and heavily one-sided. Finally, we conclude by detailing specific scenarios where the effectiveness of label smoothing is legitimately compromised. Additional resources are hosted at http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

author: Clark
title: Investigating Knowledge Distillation for Model-Agnostic Settings in Federated Learning
abstract: Can we build a generalized interface allowing arbitrary data-holders (agents) to spontaneously engage in federated learning? Any such system must operate without accessing shared representative public data while remaining completely model-agnostic, meaning it places no constraints on the specific model architecture employed by participating agents. At first glance, knowledge distillation (KD) represents the ideal mechanism for establishing these collaborative protocols. Yet, we demonstrate an unexpected result: straightforward federated learning procedures relying on KD suffer from severely degraded performance. We explore the underlying causes of this phenomenon by introducing a novel theoretical kernel ridge regression formulation tailored to federated environments, effectively capturing the dual challenges of data heterogeneity and model heterogeneity. Through this analytical lens, we prove that the observed degradation originates from a fundamental limitation inherent to knowledge distillation when confronted with data heterogeneity. To empirically substantiate our proposed framework, we construct and evaluate alternative KD-based protocols. While the actual performance attained during empirical tests using neural networks remains unsatisfactory, these quantitative results align exceptionally well with our theoretical projections.

author: Hahn
title: Applying the Pearson Correlation Coefficient to Build a Versatile Distillation Framework for Object Detection
abstract: Although creating compact architectures for object detection frequently relies on Knowledge distillation (KD), applying this procedure across heterogeneous detectors remains underexplored. Our empirical investigations reveal that a student can benefit from superior FPN features provided by a heterogeneous teacher, even when the two networks utilize distinct label assignments and detection heads. Attempting to perform distillation by straightforwardly matching feature maps, however, introduces two main challenges. Initially, excessively rigid restrictions might be imposed on the student due to discrepancies in feature magnitude relative to the teacher. Additionally, the distillation loss gradient can be heavily skewed by specific channels and FPN stages exhibiting substantial feature magnitude within the teacher model. This phenomenon introduces significant noise and obscures the contribution of alternative features during KD. To circumvent these difficulties, the proposed method leverages the Pearson Correlation Coefficient for feature imitation. This strategy mitigates strict magnitude constraints while shifting the analytical focus toward the teacher's relational information. By yielding faster convergence and functioning effectively across both heterogeneous and homogeneous student-teacher configurations, this technique consistently surpasses established KD approaches. When utilizing a robust MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, baseline performances on COCO2017 increase by 4.8% and 4.1% for FCOS and ResNet-50 based RetinaNet, culminating in respective mAP scores of 43.9% and 41.5%.

author: Walter
title: Distilling Knowledge Using Highly Capable Teacher Models
abstract: Most current knowledge distillation techniques are designed around standard configurations, utilizing training protocols and teacher models that fall short of modern state-of-the-art standards. We observe empirically that when employing a highly capable teacher, the prediction gap between student and teacher networks becomes substantially larger. Consequently, enforcing strict prediction matching through KL divergence actually harms the learning process, leading to suboptimal outcomes for conventional techniques. To effectively transfer knowledge from these highly optimized models, we demonstrate that merely maintaining the predictive relationships between the two networks is sufficient. To this end, the proposed method introduces a correlation-based loss function that directly transfers the fundamental inter-class relations of the teacher. Furthermore, recognizing that individual samples exhibit varying degrees of semantic similarity within a given category, this relational alignment is broadened to operate at the intra-class level. Despite its straightforward and practical nature, comprehensive evaluations confirm that our technique scales seamlessly across diverse model sizes, network architectures, and training strategies. It consistently achieves state-of-the-art results on object detection, image classification, and semantic segmentation benchmarks. The implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD.

author: Edwards
title: Cross-Domain Ensemble Knowledge Distillation for Secure Federated Learning
abstract: While federated learning enables local nodes to collaboratively optimize a central model without centralizing the training data, existing strategies exhibit notable vulnerabilities. Techniques that rely on co-distillation or sharing model parameters to manage imbalanced data distributions often trigger severe communication bottlenecks while introducing significant risks of privacy leakage. To address these critical flaws, the proposed method establishes a highly communication-efficient and privacy-preserving framework by leveraging offline one-shot knowledge distillation alongside unlabeled public data from an alternate domain. Within this system, fully trained local models generate local predictions, which are then combined to form a noisy and quantized ensemble. This aggregation procedure bolsters privacy guarantees without incurring any degradation in model accuracy. Extensive empirical validations on tasks in image and text classification reveal that this technique surpasses baseline federated learning algorithms, offering vastly superior communication efficiency and enhanced accuracy.

author: Rios
title: Leveraging Knowledge Distillation to Enhance Neural Topic Models
abstract: To facilitate the comprehension of massive document collections, topic models are frequently deployed to extract human-interpretable topics. Here, we integrate the key strengths of pretrained transformers and probabilistic topic models by leveraging knowledge distillation. The proposed method is highly modular and incorporates seamlessly into an arbitrary neural topic model to elevate topic quality. Demonstrating this via a pair of architecturally distinct models, we attain state-of-the-art topic coherence. Furthermore, this adaptable framework increases performance not only when averaged across all estimated topics—the standard reporting practice—but additionally during direct head-to-head evaluations contrasting aligned topics.

author: Foster
title: Distilling Knowledge from Teacher Ensembles for Click-Through Rate Prediction
abstract: Although deep learning approaches consistently elevate the accuracy of predicting the click-through rate (CTR) across diverse industrial applications, recent advancements heavily rely on constructing intricate network architectures. These complicated designs are engineered to process shifting user behaviors along with complex feature interactions. Consequently, such architectural complexity can severely impede real-time deployment by reducing the speed of online inference. Rather than designing heavier architectures, our research presents a distinct model training paradigm grounded in knowledge distillation (KD). This teacher-student framework transfers learned representations from a sophisticated teacher model directly into a student model. Applying this KD method enables the deployment of a basic, vanilla DNN as the student. Remarkably, this simplified student model attains substantial accuracy enhancements over the best existing state-of-the-art teacher models. Motivated by these profound benefits, we expand our approach to utilize a robust ensemble of multiple teachers, aiming to train an even more accurate student model. To properly integrate this multi-teacher setup for CTR prediction, we introduce innovative mechanisms, specifically utilizing distillation loss for early stopping and implementing a gating module for the teachers. We comprehensively evaluated our proposed KD training framework on three distinct industrial datasets, benchmarking it against 12 established models. Data from live online A/B testing, alongside offline evaluation metrics, confirm the practical effectiveness of the presented strategy.

author: Rocha
title: Achieving Few Shot Network Compression Through Interwoven Knowledge Distillation
abstract: To mitigate security and privacy concerns that restrict access to large training datasets, researchers increasingly explore few shot network compression. The goal is to shrink deep neural networks without substantial accuracy degradation while utilizing merely a few samples per class. Traditionally, creating lightweight models relies heavily on extensive fine-tuning data. Under these data-scarce conditions, compressed architectures are highly susceptible to over-fitting on the limited training instances. Consequently, during inference, they suffer from substantial estimation errors relative to the original model. As these deviations propagate through the model, they accumulate layer-wisely and ultimately degrade the final prediction. To combat this compounding inaccuracy, we introduce a new layer-wise knowledge distillation strategy. Our technique explicitly interweaves the hidden layers belonging to the student network and the teacher, which successfully suppresses the estimation errors that accumulate layer-wisely. Furthermore, this strategy acts as a versatile framework that readily integrates with widely used network compression methods, such as pruning. Evaluations conducted across various benchmark datasets confirm that our proposed method considerably boosts student network accuracy in scenarios where available training instances are severely restricted.

author: Ellis
title: Distilling Representations within Graph Neural Networks
abstract: To improve the capabilities of compact graph neural networks (GNNs), knowledge distillation transfers insights from highly expressive but computationally demanding teacher models into resource-efficient student models. Earlier distillation techniques for these networks introduced the Local Structure Preserving (LSP) objective, forcing the node embeddings of the student and teacher to mimic local structural relationships found along the edges. Since empirical graphs routinely contain noisy edges alongside unobserved interactions, we examine whether maintaining the broader global topology of the teacher's graph embeddings serves as a superior distillation objective for GNNs. To accomplish this, we present a contrastive learning approach that implicitly maintains global topology. It works by projecting the node embeddings of the student and the teacher into a shared representation space for alignment. Furthermore, we present new benchmarking suites comprising large empirical datasets that exhibit a substantial performance disparity between student and teacher GNNs. We evaluate our approach using 14 diverse GNN architectures and 4 distinct datasets. The results demonstrate that the proposed method reliably enhances both the resilience and accuracy of lightweight GNNs. It surpasses the original LSP, a global variant of the LSP loss, and standard baselines from 2D computer vision. By analyzing the representational similarity between the two embedding spaces, we find that our technique successfully balances the retention of local and global relationships. In contrast, prior structure-preserving methods typically excel at retaining just one of these aspects. The implementation can be accessed via https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns.

author: Baker
title: Maximizing Parallel Data Utility for Non-Autoregressive Translation by Restoring Low-Frequency Word Prediction
abstract: Training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) systems typically requires knowledge distillation (KD) to generate synthetic data. Yet, original and distilled datasets diverge regarding low-frequency words, which elevates prediction errors for these items. To mitigate this limitation, we employ pretraining to provide NAT with direct raw data exposure. Our directed alignments analysis shows that although KD deterministically maps low-frequency source words to targets, it lacks sufficient target-to-source mappings for low-frequency words. We therefore propose a reversed distillation technique to restore these missing mappings for target-side low-frequency words. Merging these methods yields a novel training framework that maximizes both synthetic and authentic data utility, further elevating NAT performance. Experiments across two advanced architectures and five translation benchmarks indicate that our strategy universally and significantly enhances translation quality by minimizing mistakes on low-frequency words. Specifically, the method attains 33.9 and 28.2 BLEU points evaluated upon the WMT16 Romanian-English and WMT14 English-German datasets. Trained models, data, and code are shared at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

author: Wright
title: Learning Semantics via Distillation to Achieve Holistic Video Scene Comprehension
abstract: Operating autonomously requires a complete grasp of the surrounding environment. Acquiring accurate ground truth labels for motion (optical flow) and geometry (depth) is notoriously difficult. Nevertheless, prior research demonstrates that deep neural networks are capable of extracting these properties from single-camera video sequences using strictly unsupervised methods. The present research advances monocular scene comprehension by integrating semantic learning with depth and optical flow estimation. To accomplish this, a pre-trained network produces surrogate ground truth images, supplying semantic supervision via knowledge distillation. The proposed method tackles these three objectives simultaneously through a lightweight neural network architecture and a unique training protocol that blends self-supervision with knowledge distillation. Consequently, the system executes efficiently across hardware extremes, from resource-constrained embedded platforms to power-intensive GPUs. Extensive evaluations confirm the framework's efficacy, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance across optical flow, motion segmentation, and monocular depth estimation tasks.

author: Hoffman
title: Knowledge Distillation within Federated Learning Frameworks
abstract: Rather than exposing their raw data, clients in typical distributed learning frameworks collaborate by transmitting model parameters. For instance, standard federated learning protocols operate by sharing the updated weights or gradients from each neural network model. Yet, this parameter exchange creates severe overhead whenever limited communication resources constrain the system, an issue worsened by the massive scale of modern deep neural networks. Federated distillation (FD) bypasses this bottleneck by communicating only the model outputs. Since output dimensions are usually minuscule compared to full network sizes (as seen with the 10 labels characterizing the MNIST dataset), FD provides an exceptionally efficient distributed learning alternative. This chapter aims to comprehensively analyze FD, emphasizing its robust communication efficiency and broad applicability across diverse tasks. To illuminate the core operational mechanisms behind FD, the first section leverages established neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory. This theoretical lens yields a new asymptotic analysis of knowledge distillation (KD) alongside co-distillation (CD)—the framework's two foundational algorithms. The following segment details a baseline FD implementation constructed specifically for classification tasks. It assesses this setup against conventional FL, detailing the resulting tradeoffs between accuracy and communication efficiency. Finally, to demonstrate the method's flexibility across various distributed learning environments, the concluding part explores two distinct applications: adapting FD for reinforcement learning and implementing it over wireless channels with asymmetric uplink-and-downlink capacities.

author: Baker
title: Merging Diverse Classifiers via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: We investigate how to consolidate expertise from multiple classifiers—each possessing a distinct architecture and distinct target classes—into one unified classifier using merely a general collection of unlabelled data. Such an operational setting naturally arises when privacy constraints prevent raw data sharing among diverse sources, restricting information exchange exclusively to privately trained models. Furthermore, varied computational resources might force these isolated sources to employ completely different neural architectures. At the same time, localized data availability heavily limits their individual capacity to comprehensively cover all target classes during the initial training phase. To address this complex challenge, we introduce a generalized form of knowledge distillation specifically tailored for merging such disparate models into a single network. Analytically, we establish a probabilistic connection linking individual model outputs to a comprehensive probability distribution spanning all target classes. Leveraging this novel connection, we develop two distinct techniques that utilize matrix factorisation and cross-entropy minimisation. These strategies allow us to approximate soft labels for every class based entirely on the unlabelled samples. These estimated soft labels then serve as highly effective substitutes for actual ground truth labels to optimize the final unified classifier. Comprehensive evaluations using the LSUN, Places365, and ImageNet datasets demonstrate that the proposed method substantially surpasses a baseline adaptation of standard distillation. Furthermore, our approach reaches an accuracy level that is nearly identical to the performance of classifiers optimized through conventional centralized, supervised training.

author: Richards
title: Applying Generative Adversarial Networks to Text Synthesis via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Because written language inherently possesses a discrete nature, replicating the high-fidelity image synthesis triumphs of generative adversarial networks (GANs) remains notoriously difficult within natural language processing. Despite this obstacle, leveraging GAN models for NLP domains—including machine translation, text summarization, and language modeling—continues to attract widespread attention. To bypass the discreteness barrier, the current paper presents a strategy that employs knowledge distillation, enabling the GAN architecture to be successfully adapted for generating text. In our pipeline, autoencoders (AEs) extract continuous sentence representations. By assigning non-zero probabilities across multiple words, these embeddings furnish a smooth representation. We subsequently distill this continuous space, guiding the generator to construct analogously smooth outputs. Empirical validation across various datasets confirms the viability of our technique. Specifically, the proposed method surpasses conventional, non-pre-trained GAN baselines during text synthesis, demonstrating elevated performance according to both the Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) metric and the BLEU score.

author: Hurst
title: Optimizing Recommender Systems Through Knowledge Distillation in Learning to Rank Architectures
abstract: To build highly efficient yet accurate recommender systems, we introduce a knowledge distillation approach specifically tailored for learning to rank tasks. While knowledge distillation has previously proven effective at balancing computational cost and predictive accuracy within image recognition, applying it directly to ranking presents unique difficulties, which our proposed framework actively resolves. In our methodology, a compact student model learns to order items and documents by utilizing standard training data alongside supervisory signals generated by a high-capacity teacher model. Because this technique remains entirely orthogonal to the specific algorithmic architectures selected for either the student or the teacher, it offers substantial structural flexibility. By significantly reducing the overall parameter count, the resulting student model dramatically accelerates online inference operations. Evaluations conducted on public datasets using state-of-the-art recommendation architectures demonstrate that our distillation strategy fulfills its primary design objectives. Specifically, when trained via our approach, the student requires under half the parameter footprint of the teacher model. Despite this massive reduction in size, it maintains a ranking performance comparable to the heavy teacher network, while simultaneously vastly outperforming an identically sized student trained independently of the distillation process.

author: Ross
title: Knowledge Distillation from Ensembles in Neural Machine Translation
abstract: Deploying a smaller model accelerates the computationally slow process of decoding sentences via Neural Machine Translation (NMT). Knowledge distillation facilitates this by leveraging a highly capable teacher network to guide the optimization of a student network. Here, we successfully condense the superior translation capabilities of an ensemble, as well as a teacher network utilizing oracle BLEU, into one standalone NMT system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that translation quality improves even if the teacher network shares identical dimensions and architecture with the student network. Because optimizing the student model remains computationally demanding, we utilize a teacher-informed data filtering method that simultaneously enhances translation outcomes and reduces training duration. Ultimately, to accelerate decoding, our approach guarantees straightforward reproducibility across arbitrary NMT architectures while avoiding any code modifications entirely.

author: Robinson
title: Addressing Deficits in Lexical Choice for Non-Autoregressive Translation Systems
abstract: Employing an autoregressive teacher model to decrease target complexity renders knowledge distillation (KD) a necessary procedure when training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) frameworks. We present empirical evidence highlighting an unintended drawback of this dependency: mistakes in lexical choice regarding low-frequency words propagate directly from the teacher model into the NAT model. To circumvent this issue, we suggest supplying the raw data directly to NAT models, which helps recover crucial information about low-frequency words that the distilled data lacks. For this purpose, we append a supplementary Kullback-Leibler divergence term, which is computed by evaluating the gap between the NAT model's lexical choice and the distribution present in the raw data. Assessments spanning diverse language pairs alongside varied model architectures underscore the generalizability and utility of the proposed methodology. Comprehensive examinations further corroborate our hypothesis, showing that overall performance improves primarily because errors in lexical choice involving rare vocabulary are successfully minimized. Promisingly, our technique advances the state-of-the-art for NAT, reaching 33.8 BLEU points on the WMT16 Romanian-English benchmark and 27.8 on the WMT14 English-German dataset. The relevant source code will be made publicly accessible.

author: Bright
title: Advancing Real-World Lipreading Through Model Efficiency and Distillation
abstract: While neural networks have driven substantial improvements in lipreading, focusing largely on optimal architecture design and enhanced generalization, current methods still fall significantly short of the constraints required for real-world implementation. To bridge this divide, our study presents multiple methodological advances. First, the application of self-distillation pushes state-of-the-art accuracy up by a substantial margin, achieving 46.6% and 88.5% on the LRW-1000 and LRW datasets, respectively. Next, we implement several structural modifications—highlighted by a newly designed head based on depthwise separable temporal convolutions—that drastically reduce the computational expense of an already highly efficient baseline. We then demonstrate how knowledge distillation serves as a powerful mechanism for regaining the accuracy lost by transitioning to these lightweight structures. Ultimately, these strategies generate a diverse set of networks offering various balances between efficiency and accuracy. Most notably, our optimal lightweight network matches the accuracy of existing state-of-the-art systems while simultaneously shrinking the parameter count by a factor of 3.9x and cutting computational cost by 8.2x. We anticipate that these results will facilitate the integration of lipreading into everyday practical applications.

author: Hicks
title: Instructing Students to Adapt: Distilling Knowledge for New Domains
abstract: Current deep learning methodologies applied to domain adaptation typically necessitate concurrent training across target and source data. This constraint renders joint training undesirable when test data distributions naturally diverge from training distributions in highly dynamic settings, such as spam filtering against evolving adversarial tactics, or when adjusting models across numerous distinct domains. To circumvent these restrictions, our proposed method extends the framework of Knowledge Distillation for use in domain adaptation tasks. Evaluating against a widely used sentiment analysis benchmark, we demonstrate that a student model can attain state-of-the-art performance during multi-source unsupervised domain adaptation. The student model achieves this by evaluating the similarity of various domains alongside the specialized proficiency of multiple teachers. Relying solely on domain similarity to estimate reliability falls short, however, when learning from an individual teacher. Consequently, we present an easily computed metric exhibiting strong correlation with target domain accuracy for that teacher. We show that isolating high-confidence examples via this newly introduced metric allows the student model to additionally capture state-of-the-art results under single-source conditions.

author: Williams
title: Data-Free Knowledge Transfer Through Adversarial Prediction Alignment
abstract: In contemporary deep learning, compressing a massive teacher network into a compact student model is widely practiced. Nevertheless, accessing the original training set is frequently impossible owing to expanding data volumes and rigorous privacy constraints. To address this, we introduce a technique that aligns the outputs of the student with the source model requiring neither metadata nor prior data. Specifically, an adversarial generator is optimized to synthesize images that maximize the predictive discrepancy between the two models. These generated samples are subsequently utilized for student training. For straightforward benchmarks such as SVHN, the compressed model achieves performance highly comparable to the original network. Furthermore, despite operating in a completely data-free regime, the proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art results on CIFAR10 for few-shot distillation scenarios restricted to 100 images per class. Additionally, we introduce an evaluation metric designed to evaluate predictive alignment between the student and teacher networks close to decision boundaries. Using this measurement, our zero-shot approach demonstrates substantially stronger alignment with the source network compared to a baseline distilled using actual training images. Our implementation is provided at https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer.

author: Rodriguez
title: Surpassing Graph Neural Networks Through a Novel Knowledge Distillation Framework
abstract: Within the machine learning domain, graph-based semi-supervised learning remains a crucial challenge. Leading classification approaches utilizing graph neural networks (GNNs) currently outperform classic techniques like label propagation. However, their intricate designs result in opaque prediction mechanisms. Consequently, these neural models fail to fully exploit essential prior knowledge present within datasets—such as the tendency for structurally linked nodes to share identical classes. To overcome these limitations, the present work introduces a knowledge distillation approach. The proposed framework captures the learned representations from any pre-trained GNN (serving as the teacher model) and transfers this information to an explicitly structured student model. By formulating the student as a jointly trainable amalgamation of parameterized feature transformation and label propagation modules, the system inherently retains prior knowledge based on both features and network structure. Consequently, the optimized student achieves enhanced predictive performance by leveraging both the teacher's expertise and the underlying data priors. Furthermore, this student model provides a prediction process that is highly interpretable compared to standard GNNs. We evaluate the proposed methodology across five standard public datasets, utilizing seven distinct GNN architectures (GLP, GCNII, SGC, SAGE, APPNP, GAT, and GCN) as teacher models. Empirical outcomes demonstrate that the optimized student reliably beats its respective teacher model by an average margin of 1.4% to 4.7%. The data and source code can be accessed at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/CPF.

author: Burton
title: Block-Structured Pruning Tailored for Hardware to Compress Large-Scale Transformer-Based Language Representations
abstract: Despite their outstanding accuracy across various tasks in natural language processing (NLP), massive pre-trained language models remain difficult to deploy, particularly given the rise of edge computing. Standard hardware platforms lack the requisite computational speed and weight storage capacity. To overcome this, we introduce a block-structured pruning strategy tailored for hardware to generate highly efficient transformer-based language representations. Our optimization pipeline specifically integrates the reweighted group Lasso algorithm. Consequently, the proposed framework substantially lowers computational overhead and weight storage demands, delivering massive compression rates. Evaluations on the GLUE benchmark for General Language Understanding Evaluation across architectures like RoBERTa, BERT, and DistilBERT demonstrate our technique reaches up to a 5.0x compression factor on specific tasks, experiencing little to no loss in accuracy. Moreover, this pruning strategy is completely orthogonal to prior compact models created via knowledge distillation. Applying our framework directly to DistilBERT yields an additional average compression rate reaching 1.79x, again with minimal accuracy degradation. Ultimately, the resulting compressed networks are highly appropriate for deployment on edge devices facing strict resource constraints.

author: Conner
title: Extracting Task-Specific Knowledge via BERT Distillation for Basic Neural Networks
abstract: Contemporary natural language processing research increasingly favors highly complex and deep architectures, exemplified by prominent language representation models such as GPT, ELMo, and BERT. Consequently, there is a widespread belief that older, shallower neural networks are no longer useful for language understanding tasks. By contrast, this work shows how fundamental, lightweight neural networks can still perform competitively. Crucially, this robust performance is achieved without introducing additional input features, relying on external training data, or requiring any architecture changes. Specifically, we transfer knowledge through distillation from the state-of-the-art BERT model into a single-layer BiLSTM. For tasks involving sentence pairs, we employ a siamese equivalent of this architecture. We evaluate this approach on tasks like natural language inference, paraphrasing, and sentiment classification over various datasets. Our proposed method yields results comparable to ELMo, yet it reduces the parameter count by a factor of roughly 100, while operating 15 times faster during inference.

author: Henderson
title: Enhancing Multi-Layer Perceptrons for Node Classification Through Knowledge Distillation from Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Despite achieving strong performance across various node classification benchmarks, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) frequently face barriers to industrial adoption. Because computing target predictions requires retrieving information from multi-hop neighborhood structures, this inherent data dependency introduces severe overhead for latency-constrained applications. Techniques typically used to accelerate inference, such as quantization and pruning, decrease overall Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations. However, because they fail to eliminate the underlying structural data dependency, their practical speedup remains restricted. Multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), on the other hand, execute significantly faster by avoiding graph dependencies entirely, though their baseline node classification accuracy typically trails that of GNNs. To exploit the contrasting advantages of both architectures, this study applies knowledge distillation (KD) to transfer predictive capabilities from GNNs into MLPs. We demonstrate that transferring knowledge from a GNN teacher drastically increases MLP performance. Because these distilled MLPs eliminate the need for graph-based inference, they yield competitive accuracy while achieving acceleration factors of 146X to 273X relative to standard GNNs, and outpace alternative acceleration strategies by 14X to 27X. Evaluated in a realistic deployment environment spanning 7 distinct datasets utilizing both inductive and transductive predictions, the proposed distilled MLPs outperform isolated MLPs by an average of 12.36% in accuracy. Furthermore, these models reach parity with their GNN counterparts on 6 out of the 7 datasets. We provide an extensive analysis detailing the mechanisms and conditions underlying these competitive results, demonstrating that distilled MLPs offer a highly effective solution for environments with strict latency constraints.

author: Brown
title: A Joint Framework for Compressing Vision Transformers
abstract: While convolutional neural networks have long been the focus of successful compression literature, research into reducing the size of Vision Transformers (ViTs) is still in its infancy. Provided they are trained on sufficiently large datasets, ViTs achieve excellent results without relying on inductive biases like convolutions. Yet, their reliance on stacked multi-head self-attention mechanisms incurs prohibitive computational costs. Furthermore, prior efforts to shrink these models typically isolate only one or two reduction strategies. To address this, the proposed method integrates knowledge distillation, layer skipping, and pruning into a single, cohesive framework for ViT compression. We construct an end-to-end optimization problem subject to explicit computational budgets. Driven by a distillation loss, this objective simultaneously optimizes the skip configurations, the layer-wise pruning masks and ratios, as well as the standard model weights. A primal-dual algorithm is then employed to solve this joint optimization task. We evaluate the proposed method on the ImageNet dataset using multiple ViT architectures, including T2T-ViT and DeiT backbones, demonstrating sustained improvements over contemporary alternatives. Specifically, our technique reduces the FLOPs of a DeiT-Tiny model by 50\% while maintaining virtually identical accuracy. Source code for this project is accessible via \url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC}.

author: James
title: Progressive Self-Distillation for Resilient Cross-Modal Representation Learning
abstract: Standard CLIP optimization exhibits notable data and compute inefficiency, largely because its learning objective fails to adequately handle the noisy many-to-many relationships typical of image captioning datasets scraped from the web. To overcome this limitation, we present a novel cross-modal contrastive training framework. By combining soft image-text alignments and progressive self-distillation, this proposed method can more efficiently extract robust representations despite the presence of noisy data. For parameter updates, the model distills internal knowledge to dynamically produce soft-alignment targets, doing so for a specific fraction of the texts and images within every minibatch. Rigorous testing on 14 benchmark datasets demonstrates that our technique consistently surpasses standard CLIP without requiring any extra computational cost. These improvements are evident across diverse settings like image-text retrieval, linear probe transfer, and zero-shot classification. Moreover, evaluations on an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed indicate that our strategy delivers greater effective robustness toward natural distribution shifts than both the original CLIP and models strictly trained on ImageNet. Finally, we performed pretraining with datasets whose sizes vary by two orders of magnitude; these results establish that our performance advantages over CLIP scale relative to the total quantity of training examples.

author: Ferrell
title: Enhancing Supernet Training via Alpha-Divergence
abstract: Finding efficient architectures automatically is often accomplished using weight-sharing NAS. This paradigm creates a unified supernet containing every candidate architecture as sub-networks, optimizing them jointly alongside the overarching model. Effective weight-sharing NAS depends heavily upon knowledge distillation from the supernet into individual student sub-networks. We discover that conventional distillation via KL divergence can cause student models to inaccurately capture teacher supernet uncertainty, resulting in either under-estimation or over-estimation, which ultimately degrades sub-network performance. To resolve this, we enhance supernet optimization by integrating the generalized alpha-divergence metric. Adaptively tuning the alpha-divergence enables us to concurrently prevent teacher uncertainty from being either under-estimated or over-estimated. Applying this alpha-divergence strategy to weight-sharing NAS as well as slimmable neural networks produces substantial empirical gains. In particular, the proposed model family generated by this technique consistently surpasses earlier architectures like Once-for-All networks, AttentiveNAS, and BigNAS across various FLOPs regimes. At a computational cost of merely 444M FLOPs, we reach 80.0% top-1 accuracy on the ImageNet benchmark. Source code as well as pretrained models have been made public at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

author: Rice
title: Broadening Fake Media Detection Capabilities Through Distillation-Based Continual Representation
abstract: Synthetic facial images and deepfakes pose critical challenges for contemporary multimedia platforms. While numerous existing algorithms identify these forgeries with high accuracy, their effectiveness drops sharply under real-world conditions because they rely heavily on static datasets and constrained evaluation environments. Traditional artificial intelligence paradigms have advanced significantly yet remain bottlenecked by stationary data assumptions. Conversely, the rapidly expanding domain of continual learning investigates how artificial algorithms might sequentially process continuous streams of related information, mirroring biological adaptability. Seeking to dramatically improve data efficiency, we bring these sequential adaptation principles into the learning dynamics of neural networks. We introduce a novel approach that synthesizes knowledge distillation, representation learning, and continual learning principles. By leveraging a teacher-student model configuration, the proposed method effectively suppresses catastrophic forgetting during sequential domain adaptation. It is specifically tailored to process incoming streams of novel deepfake content and datasets containing GAN-generated synthetic faces. Comprehensive empirical assessments confirm that our technique surpasses current state-of-the-art baselines. The results highlight its strong domain adaptation capabilities for recognizing GAN-generated imagery as well as low-quality deepfake videos spanning a variety of different datasets.

author: Maddox
title: Utilizing Earth Mover's Distance to Compress BERT Through Many-to-Many Layer Mapping
abstract: Despite their exceptional effectiveness across numerous tasks in natural language processing (NLP), pre-trained language models such as BERT face significant deployment hurdles on resource-constrained devices due to massive computational and memory requirements. We present a new BERT distillation technique utilizing a many-to-many layer mapping strategy. This configuration permits every intermediate student layer to acquire knowledge from any combination of intermediate teacher layers. Consequently, depending on the specific NLP application, the proposed architecture adaptively assimilates information from diverse teacher layers. Furthermore, the lowest total cost required to transfer knowledge from the teacher network into the student network is calculated utilizing Earth Mover's Distance (EMD). Utilizing EMD successfully facilitates the alignment necessary for this many-to-many mapping. To automatically derive the layer weights applied during the EMD calculation, we introduce an attention-based cost weighting module. This component is designed to hasten convergence time while yielding additional improvements in model performance. Comprehensive evaluations conducted on the GLUE benchmark indicate that the proposed approach delivers competitive performance against robust baselines, succeeding in both overall accuracy and effective model compression.

author: Valencia
title: A Review of Compression Techniques for Deep Learning Models in Text Applications
abstract: The domains of information retrieval (IR) alongside natural language processing (NLP) have experienced massive improvements lately, driven heavily by deep learning architectures. These innovations include standard recurrent models, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). Equally impactful are Transformer networks, including GShard, T-NLG, Text-to-text transfer transformer (T5), Extra-Long Network (XLNet), Multi-task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN), Generative Pre-training Transformer (GPT-2), and Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT). However, the enormous parameter counts of these systems conflict with the practical requirements of production environments. Deployed applications necessitate minimal power consumption, rapid inference latency, and compact memory footprints. To facilitate the integration of these massive networks into real-world industry NLP environments, this paper evaluates six distinct categories of compression strategies. Specifically, we detail Sub-quadratic Transformer techniques, Tensor Decomposition, Parameter Sharing, Knowledge Distillation, Quantization, and Pruning. Because creating compact, high-efficiency systems is essential, researchers have generated a massive volume of literature tackling this challenge. By synthesizing the extensive research produced by the deep learning NLP community over recent years, we aim to structure these fragmented developments into a logical, comprehensive overview.

author: Smith
title: Compressing Generative Adversarial Networks via Search
abstract: Deploying Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) onto mobile hardware for image translation, editing, and enhancement is highly desired, which has sparked recent interest in model reduction. Yet, while downsizing other deep models has seen massive progress, minimizing GANs (primarily their generators) is still an emerging research area. Current reduction strategies generally only function with particular architectures and objective losses. Motivated by breakthroughs utilizing AutoML for network minimization, we present a novel automated compression framework tailored for GANs. Our proposed method explores a specialized efficient search space to directly identify new lightweight generators that satisfy predefined computational budgets. The uncompressed original GAN guides this search procedure using knowledge distillation, thereby seamlessly achieving the desired compression. This approach functions entirely automatically and does not rely on a trained discriminator, making it a standalone solution compatible with a wide variety of GAN types. We assess our framework on two standard generative tasks: super resolution and image translation. Using no extra heuristics, the introduced technique produces exceptionally compact models that perform competitively and significantly surpass previous reduction methods. Source code and corresponding pretrained models are provided via https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

author: Le
title: Reassessing Embeddings of Video and Pose for the Recognition of Activities of Daily Living
abstract: Activities of Daily Living (ADL) frequently appear identical, meaning their distinction demands modeling fine-grained details. Since standard 3D ConvNets lack the flexibility to encode subtle visual patterns across actions, fusing 3D poses with RGB data remains the prevailing strategy. Yet, without specialized sensors, extracting 3D poses directly from RGB streams introduces heavy computational overhead, restricting such fusion techniques in latency-sensitive real-world settings. To optimally exploit 3D poses for ADL classification, we introduce an enhanced pose-driven attention framework investigating two distinct distillation pathways. First, we apply feature-level distillation to project pose knowledge into the RGB representations. Second, we approximate pose-driven attention by executing attention-level distillation. Both paradigms are subsequently merged into one unified architecture. We demonstrate this integrated model is highly effective, delivering substantial inference speed-ups and robust resilience against noisy poses. Whether utilizing actual 3D poses or relying exclusively on RGB, the proposed method exceeds established representative baselines evaluated on 4 public datasets. Implementation scripts are accessible at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.

author: Maldonado
title: Penultimate Feature Replication for Knowledge Distillation
abstract: To construct highly compact student networks, knowledge distillation utilizes guidance from larger teacher models. Standard algorithms typically supply the student with extra supervision derived from the soft logits of the teacher. In contrast, our research establishes that superior performance results from compelling the student to replicate the penultimate layer features of the teacher. This direct matching provides the student with highly effective information, while concurrently permitting distillation from teacher models lacking a softmax layer. Experimental evidence confirms that this technique exceeds the accuracy obtained by conventional knowledge distillation. To improve this matching procedure, we separate each feature vector into its magnitude and direction elements. We theorize that the distillation process must emphasize matching the feature direction closely, yet leave the student feature's magnitude significantly less constrained. To achieve this objective, the proposed method incorporates a distinct loss term operating via locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). Empowered by this LSH-based loss, the proposed approach precisely captures feature directions, diminishes restrictions on feature magnitudes, and yields state-of-the-art accuracy in distillation tasks. Beyond outlining theoretical analyses explaining how LSH promotes the capturing of feature directions, we broaden the proposed technique to encompass object detection and multi-label recognition domains.

author: Herrera
title: Minimizing Generative Adversarial Networks through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Applications like domain transfer, creating synthetic data, and super resolution frequently rely on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Because top-performing models require tens of millions of individual parameters, deploying them poses significant computational expenses for real-time systems or mobile hardware constrained by strict size, weight, and power (SWAP) limitations. To address the absence of prior research targeting parameter reduction in such frameworks, we introduce a knowledge distillation approach to shrink GANs, wherein a compact student GAN is trained to replicate a massive teacher GAN. Applying this distillation strategy to teacher GANs yields massive size reductions, specifically 87:1 for Celeb-A, 58:1 for CIFAR-10, and 1669:1 for the MNIST datasets, without sacrificing the visual fidelity of generated images. Our empirical findings also demonstrate that a qualitative threshold restricts the extent of allowable GAN compression. Additionally, given an identical parameter budget, GANs produced by our compression technique exhibit superior performance compared to those optimized via standard training practices. We hypothesize that this improvement stems in part from the favorable landscape for optimization inherent to over-parameterized GANs, which facilitates highly effective parameter updates via alternating gradient descent. As a result, a compact yet high-quality generative model can be achieved by initially optimizing an over-parameterized GAN and subsequently executing the proposed compression protocol.

author: Davidson
title: Improving Re-Identification Robustness via Knowledge Distillation from Multiple Views
abstract: Conventional Video-To-Video pipelines exploit tracking information to ensure resilient Re-Identification. Nevertheless, when processing isolated single image queries (such as within an Image-To-Video setting), the accuracy of these approaches degrades substantially. To mitigate this steep decline, contemporary techniques pass temporal information down from architectures operating on videos to those processing still images. Here, we formulate a training strategy enabling the distillation of enhanced knowledge extracted from a collection of diverse views capturing a target object. By structuring this visual variance as a supervisory signal inside a teacher-student framework, the proposed approach allows a teacher to guide a student model exposed to a reduced number of views. Consequently, the trained student surpasses both its teaching model and existing Image-To-Video state-of-the-art baselines significantly, achieving absolute mAP gains of 6.3% on the MARS dataset, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId, as well as a 5% increase on VeRi-776. We provide comprehensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations of the proposed method across Animal, Vehicle, and Person Re-ID tasks. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

author: Rodriguez
title: Providing Differential Privacy Guarantees for Released Graph Neural Network Models
abstract: Trained graph neural networks (GNNs) face significant privacy risks, especially as their use grows in sensitive fields such as medicine and healthcare. Specifically, even when attackers are restricted to black-box access, these trained models remain susceptible to membership inference attacks and similar vulnerabilities. To address this, we introduce a privacy-preserving strategy for releasing GNN models from a centralized setting. Given the availability of a public unlabeled graph, the proposed framework explicitly trains models on this public data while safely transferring knowledge derived from the private data. Strict privacy guarantees are achieved by integrating noisy labeling and random subsampling—two distinct noise mechanisms—into a knowledge-distillation framework. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed technique within the context of Renyi differential privacy. Finally, empirical evaluations demonstrate that our approach yields strong experimental performance when evaluated against various baselines modified for graph-structured data. The implementation can be accessed at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

author: Graham
title: Federated Learning Regularization via Hierarchical Branching
abstract: In federated learning, unequal and heterogeneous data distributions among clients pose significant difficulties, frequently causing unstable global model convergence alongside discrepancies among local networks. We introduce an architectural regularization approach designed to mitigate these issues. Within each local model, our strategy builds several secondary branches by fusing global and local subnetworks across various depth levels. Through online knowledge distillation, the primary pathway's representations are trained to align with these hybrid auxiliary branches. Without imposing any additional communication overhead, this proposed method seamlessly integrates into diverse federated learning frameworks. Furthermore, it successfully enhances global model robustness, particularly under non-iid conditions. Extensive empirical evaluations reveal that our approach achieves substantial efficiency and accuracy improvements when evaluated against current baselines. Finally, we have released our source code on the associated project website.

author: Chavez
title: Executing Data-Free Knowledge Distillation in Deep Neural Networks
abstract: While preserving nearly all predictive accuracy, contemporary techniques for model compression can successfully reduce large neural networks into significantly smaller architectures. A major limitation of these current procedures is their strict dependence on the original training set. Procuring such data is frequently unfeasible, especially when dealing with massive collections of information or when safety and privacy restrictions prevent distribution, such as in biometrics applications. To overcome this barrier, we introduce a novel approach to data-free knowledge distillation. By relying exclusively on supplementary metadata supplied alongside the pretrained model, the proposed method successfully shrinks deep neural networks that were initially optimized on extensive datasets down to a minimal proportion of their initial parameters. Finally, we analyze various forms of metadata compatible with this framework and evaluate the relative compromises associated with deploying each distinct type.

author: Mckay
title: Enhancing the Efficiency of Distilling Large-Scale Language Models
abstract:
While large-scale language models yield remarkable empirical performance today, deploying them on platforms constrained by computation and memory remains difficult. These accuracy improvements rely on massive parameter counts, high power consumption, and slower inference speeds. Compressing these massive networks is frequently achieved using the knowledge distillation (KD) framework. However, when task-specific data is scarce, the student model struggles to extract sufficient guidance from the teacher model. Furthermore, slight shifts in data distribution often produce inconsistent predictions, because massive neural network architectures are highly susceptible to memorizing the training instances.

To mitigate these challenges, we introduce a novel distillation framework that is data-agnostic and utilizes mixup—a straightforward yet effective data augmentation technique—yielding better generalization capabilities for the compressed network. Specifically, our proposed method trains the student model to replicate the teacher's behavior not only on standard training examples but also on linear interpolations of paired examples. We mathematically prove that, assuming reasonable conditions, this approach minimizes the gap between the empirical error and the generalization error. Our framework is evaluated using the GLUE benchmark to confirm its efficacy, where it provides substantial, consistent improvements compared to standard KD training and surpasses multiple competitive baselines. Finally, ablation studies and evaluations in limited-data scenarios additionally validate the benefits of this approach.

author: Liu
title: Equipping CLIP for Multimodal Generation Through Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Models leveraging massive image-text datasets for vision-language pre-training (VLP), such as the dual-stream architecture CLIP, excel across diverse multimodal alignment tasks. Yet, a weak text encoder leaves these systems unable to handle multimodal generative tasks. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a technique that fuses a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) into the dual-stream VLP architecture using vision-language knowledge distillation. This proposed distillation strategy unlocks generative abilities while remaining highly data-efficient and computation-efficient when compared against from-scratch pre-training. Empirical evaluations demonstrate robust zero-shot performance for our augmented framework on applications like image captioning and open-ended visual question answering. Notably, on the VQAv2 benchmark, the framework yields a zero-shot accuracy of 44.5%, exceeding the prior state-of-the-art zero-shot baseline while requiring $7\times$ fewer parameters. Finally, our distillation approach preserves the native text generation and understanding skills of the PLM, yielding a versatile system capable of executing unimodal as well as multimodal tasks.

author: Mason
title: Optimizing Student Networks by Means of Feature Embedding
abstract: Despite their widespread success across numerous domains, deploying deep convolutional neural networks on mobile devices remains challenging due to their severe computational and storage costs. Knowledge distillation addresses this limitation by transferring expertise from a cumbersome, well-trained teacher network to a highly efficient student network. Historically, teacher-student architectures aligned intermediate layers by inserting extra fully-connected layers, a practice that inevitably introduces massive amounts of auxiliary parameters. Instead, the proposed method bypasses this drawback by transmitting information between models without creating any new variables requiring optimization. We re-examine this distillation paradigm strictly through the framework of feature embedding. By employing a locality preserving loss, we force the student network to output low-dimensional features that successfully capture the intrinsic properties present in the corresponding high-dimensional features of the larger model. As a result, the lightweight model naturally sustains the predictive accuracy of the teacher network. Alongside our empirical results, theoretical analysis verifies the reduced computation complexity of this strategy. Finally, extensive experiments on standard benchmark datasets using optimized models demonstrate that the proposed technique outperforms current state-of-the-art teacher-student approaches regarding both storage limitations and computational overhead.

author: White
title: Image-to-Image Translation Using Compact Generative Adversarial Networks Created Via Distillation
abstract: Standard network compression techniques typically address visual recognition rather than generation tasks. Consequently, while Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) see widespread application for image-to-image translation, their substantial storage and computation requirements severely limit deployment on mobile devices. Drawing on concepts from knowledge distillation, we train a student generator possessing fewer parameters by transferring both high-level and low-level information from a massive teacher generator. We construct an adversarial learning process to jointly optimize a newly introduced student discriminator alongside this student generator. Specifically, to enhance the student generator's capabilities, the student discriminator evaluates the distances separating real images, outputs from the teacher generator, and those from the student generator. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations on benchmark datasets indicate that our proposed method successfully yields portable generative models while maintaining strong performance.

author: Gaines
title: Task-Oriented Compression of BERT Utilizing Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
abstract: BERT and similar pre-trained language models excel across many natural language processing applications, but their massive parameter counts complicate deployment in resource-constrained environments demanding real-time inference. Current approaches shrink these networks independently of the downstream application, yielding a single compressed BERT variant for every situation. Emphasizing the value of customizing architectures, we present a compression strategy utilizing differentiable Neural Architecture Search for autonomously generating compact, task-adaptive configurations. To establish an optimal balance between effectiveness and computational efficiency, the proposed method utilizes an efficiency-aware loss to enforce search constraints, alongside search hints derived from a knowledge distillation loss targeted at specific tasks. Evaluations conducted on multiple NLP tasks indicate that our dynamically tailored architectures preserve comparable performance. Simultaneously, they shrink the parameter size by factors of 11.5x to 17.0x and accelerate inference by 12.7x to 29.3x relative to standard BERT.

author: Harrell
title: Accommodating Every Node: Comprehensive Federated Learning Across Devices with Heterogeneous Compute
abstract: Extracting robust global models utilizing decentralized data while maintaining privacy makes federated learning (FL) an essential strategy. Standard FL techniques generally presume that all clients can locally optimize the exact same global architecture. Practical deployments heavily contradict this assumption because edge computing power exhibits substantial hardware heterogeneity. Consequently, incorporating successful but massive networks like BERT becomes highly problematic when utilizing computationally restricted nodes. Trivial mitigation strategies generally involve deploying an intrinsically small model everywhere or entirely ignoring participants lacking sufficient hardware.
